p: Nadia Brooks found the note at ten to six, when she went looking for coffee in an apartment that still smelled like cardboard. Her sister Callie had driven up from Pueblo on Saturday in a borrowed truck with Rosie buckled in the back, carried boxes for six hours, and left before dark, because the drive home was close to two hours now. It used to be one.

Sticky note on the coffee maker. Coffee's in the cabinet left of the sink. Rosie's rocket is on the fridge. She says yours needs a bathroom and a window. I've got Dad. Call him Friday anyway. He says he isn't counting. He's counting. Don't get so busy up there you forget the way down here. C

The rocket was purple, with four stick people in the window, because Nadia had told Rosie on Saturday it was for four astronauts. Rosie had asked where they'd sleep. Nadia hadn't known. She stood in the kitchen looking at it longer than she meant to, then made the coffee.
At 6:40 she sat in her car in the Front Range Orbital lot and watched the sun come up behind a sign that still said Centennial Lighting Works.

The company had bought the old factory two years ago and never taken the sign down. Somebody had added a sticker under it, a little drawing of a space station, and that was the rebrand. Inside, she'd been told, was a high bay big enough to stand a city bus on its end, a pressure test cell, and four hundred people who built things that held air.

Her badge said Systems Engineer. She had never been one. For five years she had been a test engineer at an avionics shop in Colorado Springs, the person who wrote the procedure, ran the unit through it, and signed the sheet that said it passed. She was good at it. She was fast and careful and she never fudged a number.

She knew exactly why she'd picked that work. Her father had climbed poles for Xcel until the year he stopped, the year she was nine, and nobody in the house talked about that year. What she took from it was simple. A check that passed was the only thing that let anybody sleep.
Her phone buzzed. Dad, thirty one years on the lines, and these days he texted only in capital letters.
A text from Dad. FIRST DAY. PROUD OF YOU. REMEMBER YOU DONT CLIMB A POLE YOU HAVENT GROUNDED.
She smiled, typed back a heart, and went inside.

By nine she was in a conference room with a whiteboard that still had a lighting fixture wiring diagram ghosted under the erasures. At the head of the table sat Wes Harland, the chief engineer, fifty eight, sleeves rolled, the man who had designed more pressure vessels than anyone in the building. Amara Osei, the program manager, had the signed contract open on her laptop. Tiago Ferreira from integration and test leaned against the wall with a coffee. A young engineer named Jun Takeda had a laptop covered in stickers and an open modeling tool.

Halo Orbital signed Friday, Amara said. HEARTH. A habitat module for their station. Ninety cubic meters, crew of four, fifteen year design life, launch in thirty months. Firm fixed price on development. This is the biggest thing this company has ever won, and the people who will sleep in it are astronauts.
It's a can with air in it, Wes said. We've built eleven cargo modules. We know what to build. I'd like a layout on this board by Friday.
Everyone looked at the new systems engineer. Nadia thought about her father, and about how sure that crew had been.
Colleen's Flight Notes: start with the problem.
What a systems engineer is for.

Colleen Whitcomb met her at a diner on Arapahoe Road that afternoon and ordered pie for both of them. Nadia had met her four years ago, when Colleen was the Air Force pilot flying the evaluation flights on the displays Nadia's shop tested. After one debrief Nadia had stayed behind and asked her what the cold start test was actually for. Colleen had looked at her for a long second and then told her. She'd retired since, joined FRO's advisory board, and put Nadia's name in front of Wes.

Nadia told her about Wes and the can with air in it. Colleen listened without interrupting. Then she pulled a napkin over. You were the only tester at that shop who ever asked me what a test was for, she said. That's why you're here. That's the whole job.

Systems engineering is a way of making sure a whole thing works, for the people who need it, across its whole life. A system is a set of parts that interact to do something none of them can do alone. That last part is the point. A habitat module is a pressure shell, an air system, a thermal loop, power, data, crew quarters, and a hatch. None of those keeps four people alive. Together they might. The behavior that only shows up when the parts work together is called emergent behavior, and it's where both the value and the surprises live. Systems thinking means looking at the whole, the interactions, and the environment the system lives in, instead of one part at a time.
Wes is right that he knows how to build a can, Colleen said. Your job is to make sure it's the right can.

How the exam asks it. Expect definition questions. If an answer talks about the whole, the interactions, the stakeholders, and the full life cycle, it's usually the systems engineering answer. If it optimizes one part in isolation, it usually isn't.
The life cycle and its gates.

Colleen drew six boxes on the napkin. Every system moves through life cycle stages. The handbook's generic set is Concept, Development, Production, Utilization, Support, and Retirement. Concept is where you figure out what's needed and whether it's feasible. Development is where you define, design, build, verify, and validate it. Production makes it, Utilization is when people use it, Support keeps it working, and Retirement takes it out of service and disposes of it. Utilization and Support run side by side. HEARTH will spend fifteen years in those two stages, and somebody will eventually have to plan how it leaves orbit with the station.

Between stages sit decision gates. A gate is a planned point where leaders look at the evidence and decide what happens next. The options aren't just yes or no. They can proceed to the next stage, proceed with action items to close, keep working in the current one, go back to an earlier stage, put the project on hold, or end it. Technical reviews, like a system requirements review or a preliminary design review, feed those decisions with evidence. A gate is where you're allowed to say we're not ready, Colleen said. Use it.
How the exam asks it. Know the six generic stages in order, and know that Utilization and Support overlap. Know that a gate decision can be more than proceed or stop.

Then she drew a V. Down the left side you define: stakeholder needs, system requirements, architecture, design. At the bottom you build. Up the right side you integrate and prove: parts into subsystems, subsystems into the system, verifying each level against its own requirements as you go, and validating the whole against the stakeholders' needs at the top. Every level on the left has a partner on the right. The requirement you write on the way down is the thing you test on the way up. A test answers whatever question somebody wrote down, she said. Your job is making sure somebody wrote down the crew's.

The handbook organizes the work into four process groups from ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288. Agreement processes cover buying and supplying. Organizational project-enabling processes give projects what they need: life cycle models, infrastructure, portfolios, people, quality, and knowledge. Technical management processes plan, assess, decide, and control. Technical processes do the engineering, from mission analysis all the way to disposal. Verification asks whether you built it right, against the requirements. Validation asks whether you built the right thing, for the stakeholders, in the real environment.
How the exam asks it. Verification and validation questions are everywhere on this exam. Requirements go with verification. Stakeholder needs and intended use go with validation.
Mission analysis comes before the layout.

The first technical process is business or mission analysis. Its purpose is to define the problem or opportunity, characterize the solution space, and identify the kinds of solutions that could work. You ask why the system should exist, who it serves, what success looks like, and what constraints you can't move. You produce a problem statement and early life cycle concepts, including how it will be operated, before anyone draws a layout. For HEARTH that means asking what Halo is really trying to do with this module, not just what the contract volume is.

Planning starts in the first week too. Project planning produces the plans, and for the engineering work that's usually a systems engineering management plan, or SEMP. It says which processes you'll use, how you'll tailor them, what reviews you'll hold, who owns what, and how technical work ties to the schedule. Wes wants a layout by Friday, Colleen said, finishing the pie. Give him something better by Friday. Give him the problem.
How the exam asks it. If a question describes a team jumping to a design before the problem is defined, the best answer goes back to mission analysis and stakeholder needs.
Decision one. A layout by Friday.

Wes was already at the whiteboard with a marker. He drew a long cylinder, a hatch on one end, and started sketching four boxes along one wall. Crew quarters here. Galley in the middle. Hygiene on the far end so it's away from the food. Test kid, you can start tracking the mass.
It took her a second to realize the test kid was her. Jun glanced at her. Tiago raised an eyebrow over his coffee. What does Nadia do?
A. Start a mass tracker on Wes's layout and keep it current all week.
B. Let Wes keep sketching and draft a list of open questions on the side.
C. Tell Wes in front of the team that the layout is coming too early.
D. Ask Wes for two days to write up Halo's mission and constraints.

Wes grunts. Two days. Nadia reads Halo's business plan, the station design guide, and the mission profile, and puts one page on his desk Wednesday night: what Halo is trying to do, how a crew will use the module, and the constraints nobody can move. Wes reads it twice and doesn't say anything. He also doesn't erase it.

That's the move. Business or mission analysis defines the problem and the solution space before anyone commits to a solution. It's quick when you do it early and very expensive when you skip it. You didn't fight Wes. You gave him a better starting line.
Tuesday morning Amara put the program schedule on the screen. It started with contract award and went straight to a preliminary design review in month four.
The contract's signed, so we're past the concept stuff, she said. We don't need a mission concept review or a requirements review. Halo already bought the module. I want to save the six weeks.
A. Agree to drop both reviews and win back the six weeks for design.
B. Hold both reviews at full scale from the old government handbook.
C. Ask Halo's program office whether FRO should hold the early reviews.
D. Fold the two reviews into one short gate sized to HEARTH's risk.

Amara pushes back, then agrees to a combined review in week six, one day long, with clear entry and exit criteria. It costs her two weeks instead of six, and she gets a written baseline she can hold Halo to.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Life cycle stages end in decision gates, and the gate is where you're allowed to say not yet. Tailoring means right sizing the review, not deleting it. You kept the decision and cut the overhead.
Amara stopped by Nadia's desk after lunch. I have a schedule. I don't have an engineering plan. Halo's contract asks for one in thirty days. What do you need from me?
Nadia had written test plans. She had never written a plan for how an entire program does its engineering.
A. Add an engineering column with owners and review dates to Amara's schedule.
B. Draft a SEMP from the handbook outline, with each tailoring choice explained.
C. Rename FRO's last cargo module SEMP for HEARTH and send it to Halo on time.
D. Write the SEMP once the first design review has settled the baseline.

She builds it from the handbook outline, borrowing what still fits from the cargo SEMP and marking every tailoring choice with a reason. Amara reads the review section, adds two milestones to her schedule, and says, Now I can defend this.

Exactly right. Project planning produces the plans that tell everyone how the technical work will happen. The SEMP is the engineering half of that. Writing tailoring decisions down, with reasons, is what separates tailoring from skipping.
FRO had a binder. Literally a binder, three inches thick, called the Product Development Process. Wes had written most of it ten years ago for cargo modules. Every program at FRO followed it.

Reading it Wednesday night, Nadia found what she half expected. There was no step for a crew safety review, no human factors evaluation, nothing about a hazard report. The binder had been built for modules that carried food and spare parts.
A. Run HEARTH from the INCOSE handbook directly and set the binder aside.
B. Take the gap to the binder's owner with a proposed crewed tailoring.
C. Write the missing crew safety steps into her personal checklist.
D. Follow the binder as written and log the missing crew steps as a risk.
The owner turns out to be Wes. He reads her two pages, grumbles about the length, and signs it. Should have done this when we bid it. The binder gets a new tab: crewed programs.

That's the move. Life cycle model management means the organization owns its processes and improves them deliberately. When a new kind of program shows up, you change the model through its owner. Next time the steps are already there.
Decision five. Who cares about this module.
Jun had started a stakeholder list in the model. It had two names on it: Halo Orbital and FRO.
That's who signed the contract, he said. Who else is there?
A. Widen the list to everyone HEARTH touches, from launch to disposal.
B. Add the astronauts as the real users and leave the rest to Amara's team.
C. Ask Halo for its own stakeholder list and adopt it for HEARTH.
D. Keep the two contract parties for now and add others as they come up.

The list grows to fourteen. Jun adds a column for what each one needs and another for how they'd know the module works. Two of the fourteen, the station's robotic arm team and the disposal planners, have requirements nobody had heard of.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Stakeholder identification covers the whole life cycle: users, operators, maintainers, regulators, interfacing systems, and the people who'll retire it. Each brings needs, and missing needs become missing requirements.

Thursday, reading the statement of work line by line, Nadia found a sentence that bothered her. "Habitable volume shall be at least 90 cubic meters." There was no definition of habitable volume anywhere in the contract.
Pressurized volume, the inside of the shell, was about ninety. Habitable volume, the space a person can actually move in after the racks and quarters are installed, would be a lot less.
A. Grow the module until it meets either reading of habitable volume.
B. Call Helen at Halo and design to the definition she gives.
C. Design to the pressurized volume HEARTH already meets.
D. Ask Amara to send Halo a formal request to define the term.

Amara sends a formal clarification request through the contracts channel that afternoon. Halo's answer comes back in a week, in writing, and it's the habitable reading. Nadia is glad she asked in week one instead of month nine.

Exactly right. In the supply process, the supplier makes sure it understands what the acquirer is asking for and that the agreement says it clearly. Ambiguity gets resolved through the agreement, in writing, early.

By Thursday afternoon Nadia had found three versions of the HEARTH mission profile. One was on Wes's laptop, one was attached to an email chain, and one was printed and pinned to the wall in the high bay with handwritten notes.
They disagreed about how long the crew stays. Ninety days on Wes's laptop. A hundred and eighty on the wall, in somebody's handwriting.
A. Name Wes's laptop copy the master and tell the team to use it.
B. Send everyone the newest version, and ask them to delete the rest.
C. Set up one controlled repository with an owner for each document.
D. Keep a page in her notebook tracking which version is current.

It takes a day of setup and a short note to the team. Tiago is the first to move his test documents in. The pinned printout in the high bay gets a sticky note on it: "Current version lives here," with a link.

That's the move. Information management makes sure the right people have the right information, current and controlled, for the whole life cycle. On a fifteen year program, where things live is an engineering decision.
Decision eight. Saying it to Wes.

By Thursday evening the pattern was clear. Wes made calls fast, and his calls were usually right, and nobody ever asked him why. Nadia had three things she needed to raise with him: the layout, the binder, and the volume question.
She was thirty one. He'd been building pressure vessels since before she was born. Her stomach did the thing it always did before she told somebody senior they might be wrong.
A. Ask Wes for twenty minutes alone and hear his view on each first.
B. Wait a few months, build some credibility, then raise all three.
C. Bring the three issues to Amara and let her decide what goes to Wes.
D. Lay out all three issues in an email to Wes with Amara copied.

Wes talks for fifteen of the twenty minutes, about a cargo module in 2019 that leaked at the hatch seal and how he found it. Then he listens. On the volume question he says, Good catch. On the layout he says, Fine. Give me your problem statement. But I'm not waiting forever.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Systems engineering is a team sport, and influence is part of the job. Go to the person first, privately, with curiosity before conclusions. You learned something from him, and he heard you because you asked first.
Decision nine. The test engineer's instinct.

Tiago pulled up a chair Friday morning. You're a test person. I'm a test person. Let's get ahead of it. Help me start the verification plan now and we'll be the only program at FRO that isn't scrambling at the end.
It was exactly what Nadia was good at, and she felt the pull. She also knew what she was reaching for: the moment a test came back green and everybody got to go home.
A. Start drafting the verification plan with Tiago this week.
B. Work with Tiago on how Halo will decide HEARTH works for a crew.
C. Ask Tiago to hold test planning until the design is done at CDR.
D. Ask Halo to define the acceptance tests HEARTH will have to pass.
Tiago thinks about it and grins. Validation first. I like it. They draft four questions for Halo about how a crew will actually live in and leave the module, and the first one is about a fire.

Exactly right. Validation asks whether you built the right thing for its intended use. Setting validation intent early means the requirements, and then the verification, point at what the crew actually needs.
Amara needed a drafter for Wes's layout drawings and had Jun's name on a sticky note.

Jun had told Nadia on Tuesday that he'd joined FRO to do model-based systems engineering, and that this was the first program where anyone had let him open the modeling tool. He had a SysML model of the stakeholder list already. He'd built it on his own time.
A. Encourage Jun to make his own case to Amara for the model work.
B. Split Jun's week between Wes's drawings and the system model.
C. Make the case to Amara for putting Jun on the system model.
D. Let Amara put Jun on drafting for the first quarter of the program.

Amara agrees, on the condition Nadia finds her a drafter. Nadia does, a contractor Tiago knows. Jun gets the model and a development plan with two milestones on it. He brings Nadia a coffee the next morning without saying why.
That's the move. Projects need the right people with the right competencies, and people need to grow. You matched the skill to the work, solved the manager's real problem, and invested in someone.
At Friday's staff meeting Nadia suggested inviting someone from FRO's tiny safety office and a human factors specialist to the concept work.
Safety reviews the design, test kid, Wes said. They don't make it. They'll get it at PDR like always.
A. Bring safety and human factors into the concept work starting this week.
B. Write the first hazard list herself and bring the specialists in at PDR.
C. Leave the first safety review at PDR where FRO's binder puts it.
D. Have safety review the concept once it's written, well ahead of PDR.
The safety engineer is a quiet woman named Odette. In the first meeting she asks one question, where the crew goes if the air goes bad, and nobody has an answer. Now it's on the list.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Quality characteristics, like safety and human systems integration, get designed in. On a crewed program they belong in the concept, because the cheapest time to remove a hazard is before anyone has drawn it.
Friday at four, Halo's director of crew operations called in for a get-to-know-you. Helen Cho-Ramirez had spent eleven years as a flight surgeon for long duration crews, and she didn't waste time.

I read your contract. It says ninety cubic meters. That's not what I need. I need four people to live in there for six months, and if there's a fire in the galley at three in the morning, I need all four of them to get out, or to a safe place, before the smoke gets them. I don't see that anywhere in the paperwork.
A. Tell Helen the need isn't in the contract and would take a change order.
B. Promise Helen a safe haven and two egress paths in the design.
C. Write the need down in Helen's words and ask her to walk through it.
D. Ask Helen to send the need in writing through Halo's program office.

Nadia asks three follow up questions: how long smoke takes to become dangerous, where Helen thinks the crew sleeps, and what the old station did. Helen answers all three in detail. At the end she says, Call me after you've timed it.

Exactly right. A stakeholder need, stated in the stakeholder's words, is gold. Capture it, understand it, and take it into needs and requirements definition, where it can be traced and, if needed, handled through the agreement. Don't dismiss it and don't promise around it.

Nadia stayed late Friday. She opened a new document in the repository she had set up on Thursday, titled it HEARTH Stakeholder Needs, and typed Helen's words exactly as Helen had said them, three in the morning and all.

It had been a good week, and she knew it. She'd given Wes a problem instead of a fight, kept the gates without wasting the schedule, and gotten the volume question in writing before anyone built to the wrong number. On his way out Wes stopped at her desk. Night, Brooks. She was halfway to the car before she noticed.
On the drive home she called her father. He picked up on the first ring, the way he always did.
So, he said. They figure out what they hired yet?

I think I found a question nobody's asked, she said. She told him about Helen, about the galley fire at three in the morning, about four people in a can two hundred and fifty miles up with nowhere to go.
He was quiet for a while. He went quiet like that whenever work got anywhere close to the year he stopped climbing.
Then that's your job, he said. Somebody's got to be the one who asks where they go.
Then his voice changed, the way it did when he got to the part he'd been saving. Rosie wants to know if you live in space now. I told her not yet.
Nadia laughed, and it caught a little on the way out. She told him she'd come down soon. Okay, he said. He'd heard that one before. He said okay anyway.
Monday morning Helen's email was waiting.

An email from Helen Cho-Ramirez. Subject: Following up on fire and safe haven. Nadia,. Thank you for Friday. I've attached the old station's emergency response times for fire and depressurization, and a sketch of where I think the crew sleeps. On the old station we timed it once: bunk to hatch, lights out, alarm going. Nobody has timed yours. I want that number before anybody draws a wall.. Helen
